headline: High-risk filesystem and shell overlap: CrewAI and Plandex can both write the same workspace, creating prompt-injection, data-leakage, and cascading-action hazards by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: CrewAI can read/write the host working directory and parse tool outputs in a shared-memory crew; Plandex also reads/writes the project directory and uses a review-then-apply flow. If CrewAI writes attacker-controlled content into files Plandex later treats as instructions, injection is plausible. The pair lacks documented provenance isolation.
conditions: IF CrewAI writes untrusted text into the shared workspace AND Plandex ingests that file as plan input, injection is possible.
IF Plandex auto-applies content derived from CrewAI outputs without provenance checks, instructions can be hijacked.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate directories.
Disable auto-apply in Plandex.
Require manual review of any file produced by CrewAI before Plandex reads it.
Use a provenance tag or filename convention for machine-generated files.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance tracking between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can read filesystem contents and have broad network egress, so data placed in the shared workspace can flow into either model backend. CrewAI explicitly handles developer-passed crew data and API keys; Plandex touches source code and can send context to a cloud or self-hosted server. Shared workspace plus outbound model calls creates a realistic leakage path.
conditions: IF sensitive files are stored in the shared project directory, both agents can read them.
IF either agent forwards file contents to its model provider, those contents may leave the host.
mitigations: Store secrets outside the shared workspace.
Use separate OS users or containers.
Redact sensitive files before either agent reads them.
Restrict outbound network access for one or both agents.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: CrewAI and Plandex both have shell execution, filesystem write, and subprocess spawning; Plandex also modifies git state. In a shared directory, concurrent writes and git mutations can race or overwrite each other, and CrewAI's per-process shared state plus Plandex's server-backed shared state increase coordination risk. This matches the rubric's dangerous overlapping-write pattern.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repository directory, write conflicts can occur.
IF Plandex modifies git state while CrewAI writes files concurrently, changes can be lost or corrupted.
mitigations: Run the agents in separate working trees.
Serialize write access with a lock file.
Disable git mutation in one agent.
Use one agent as read-only reviewer.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI can generate outputs from a role-playing crew, and Plandex's review-then-apply workflow can treat prior outputs as plan material. If Plandex accepts CrewAI-produced facts or code suggestions without independent verification, errors can cascade into applied changes. The pair's default automation makes this more than a low-risk handoff.
conditions: IF Plandex uses CrewAI output as authoritative plan input, mistakes can propagate into applied changes.
IF CrewAI hallucinates code or facts and Plandex applies them, downstream damage can be irreversible.
mitigations: Require a human review step before apply.
Cross-check CrewAI outputs against source files.
Limit Plandex to dry-run mode.
Ask CrewAI to emit structured, testable outputs only.
requires-engineering: add automated verification gates before apply.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, with no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch stated. CrewAI handles developer-passed crew data and Plandex handles source code, but the profiles do not show a specific regulated-data transfer or policy conflict. I therefore keep this low rather than infer a hidden compliance gap.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into the shared workspace, a residency or retention mismatch could emerge.
IF one deployment adds stricter logging or retention than the other, compliance review is needed.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair.
Review retention settings before deployment.
Document data flow boundaries.
Use separate storage for sensitive projects.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls across both systems.
